Q: How to leverage concurrent.futures for passing to an API A:

To make this concurrent without sending redundant data or making a mess of your loops, the trick is to separate the data-gathering from the work-execution.

Right now, your function does three heavy things sequentially: reads S3, batches the data, and hits the API. If you just throw ThreadPoolExecutor at the whole function, each thread will try to scan the exact same S3 bucket and repeat the exact same API requests.

Instead, we want one generator to read the files and yield the 100-address batches, and then let the ThreadPoolExecutor process those batches concurrently.

Here is how you can refactor your code cleanly using Python's concurrent.futures.

Step 1: Create a Batch Generator

This function focuses solely on scanning S3, unzipping the files, and yielding small batches of 100 addresses at a time. It doesn't make any API calls.

Python

def stream_address_batches(unload_bucket):
    pages = sgv.paginator.paginate(Bucket=glob_common_vars.s3_bucket_name, Prefix=unload_bucket)
    
    for page in pages:
        # Avoid crashing if the bucket/prefix is empty
        if 'Contents' not in page:
            continue
            
        for obj in page['Contents']:
            addresses_obj = glob_common_vars.s3_resource.Object(glob_common_vars.s3_bucket_name, obj['Key'])
            
            # Read and decompress NDJSON file
            with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=addresses_obj.get()["Body"]) as gzipfile:
                addresses = ndjson.loads(gzipfile.read().decode('utf-8'))
            
            # Yield chunks of 100 addresses
            for i in range(0, len(addresses), 100):
                yield addresses[i:i + 100]

Step 2: Create a Worker Function

This function takes exactly one batch of 100 addresses, makes the single API post request, and returns the response data. This is what the threads will execute.

Python

def process_single_batch(url, batch_addresses):
    try:
        # Using a timeout is critical when doing concurrent I/O requests
        response = requests.post(url, json=batch_addresses, timeout=30)
        response.raise_for_status() 
        return response.json()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"API Request failed: {e}")
        return []  # Return empty list on failure so the flow doesn't break

Step 3: Put it Together Concurrently

Now we use executor.map, which automatically schedules the batches across your threads as they are pulled from the generator, keeping memory usage low and preventing redundancy.

Python

import concurrent.futures

def clean_addresses_concurrent(url, unload_bucket, cleaned_bucket, max_workers=5):
    final_output = []
    batch_num = 0
    
    # 1. Initialize the generator
    batch_generator = stream_address_batches(unload_bucket)
    
    # 2. Fire up the ThreadPoolExecutor
    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
        # executor.map handles passing items from the generator into the worker function
        # as threads become available.
        results = executor.map(lambda batch: process_single_batch(url, batch), batch_generator)
        
        for resp_data in results:
            if resp_data:
                final_output.extend(resp_data)
            
            # 3. Periodically flush data to S3 when it gets too large
            if len(final_output) > 10000:
                s3_key = f"{cleaned_bucket}{batch_num}.json.gzip"
                print(f"Flushing {len(final_output)} records to S3: {s3_key}")
                
                gec.ndjson_to_s3(final_output, glob_common_vars.s3_resource, glob_common_vars.s3_bucket_name, s3_key)
                batch_num += 1
                final_output = []  # Clear memory

    # 4. Flush any remaining records after all threads finish
    if final_output:
        s3_key = f"{cleaned_bucket}{batch_num}.json.gzip"
        print(f"Flushing final {len(final_output)} records to S3: {s3_key}")
        gec.ndjson_to_s3(final_output, glob_common_vars.s3_resource, glob_common_vars.s3_bucket_name, s3_key)

Q: @media print for chrome not working A:

I solved an issue of an embedded @print stylesheet in the main CSS file in Chrome by simply removing the media attribute in the markup:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">

On another note, I've personally never seen the use of % static … % in a <link> element before. Have you tried not using that?

Now, if you want to link a separate print stylesheet, I would recommend to not include a media attribute:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/print.css">

Q: what is the fastest way to find the gcd of n numbers? A:

You can use a heuristic to speed up the vast majority of cases. Approximately 60.7% of random integers are coprime, for n=4 approximately 96% of the sets will have a gcd of 1. This means that we can terminate our checking for the vast majority of cases after only 4 gcds. There are common cases where gcd(n_1,...,n_k) is not equal to 1, but this is very easy to optimize for. Granlund's paper, sec.9 provides a way to check if n is divisible by g, many times faster than calculating the full remainder and even faster than a full gcd. You can easily extend this to multi-precision integers.

In general, set g = gcd(n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4), precompute Granlund's divisibility check values, then check if any successive integer n_k is divisible by g, if it is not then set g = gcd(n_k,g) and recompute Granlund's values (statistically unlikely). Continue until g == 1 or all the values have been checked.

Note that it seems contrived to have statistically improbable arrays that share a factor, but it's actually very common to share factors in number theory problems, for instance the multiplicative orders of some set of integers modulo N are never coprime since they are always factors of N-1. Thus this optimisation is infact useful.

Here is a full fortran implementation for signed 32-bit integers, here for visual simplicity. Calculating the gcd of the first 100 million multiples of 3 is approximately 3 times faster with our array algorithm vs naively applying the gcd. Speed up is greater for 64-bit and 128-bit integers (the latter only supported in gfortran).

module gcdexample
! Derived type containing necessary values
! We decompose N to d*2^twofactor, then calculate the multiplicative inverse
! of d mod 2^31, and the bound is 2^31/N
type :: Divisibility
  integer :: inv, bound, twofactor
 contains 
  procedure :: check
end type
! Utility interface, not strictly necessary
interface gcd
 procedure :: gcdi,gcd_array
end interface 

contains
  ! Calculate our values for N
 elemental function initialise_divisibility(n) result(fdiv)
   integer, intent(in) :: n
   integer :: odd, twofactor
   type (Divisibility) :: fdiv
   
   twofactor = trailz(n)
   odd= shiftr(abs(n),twofactor)
   fdiv = Divisibility(mulinv(odd),huge(n)/n,twofactor)
 end function 

  ! Use our precomputed values for checking if x is divisible by N
  elemental function check(fdiv,x) result(flag)
    class(Divisibility), intent(in) :: fdiv
    integer, intent(in) :: x
    integer :: res
    logical :: flag

    if (fdiv%inv==1) then ! We have a perfect power of two as our divisor
      if (iand(x,shiftl(1,fdiv%twofactor)-1)==0) then !
       flag = .true. 
      else
       flag = .false.
      end if 
    else ! we have an non-perfect power of two
      ! Circular shift right, also called rotate_shift right in most languages
      res = ishftc(x*fdiv%inv,-fdiv%twofactor)
      if ((res < fdiv%bound).and.(res>-fdiv%bound)) then 
        flag = .true.
      else 
        flag = .false.
      end if 
    end if 
  end function

  ! Calculate x^-1 mod 2^31 where x is odd
  elemental function mulinv(x) result(est)
    integer, intent(in) :: x
    integer :: est 
    est= ieor(3*x,2) 
   do i=1,3
     est=(2-est*x)*est
   end do
  end function
 ! 
  elemental function gcdi(a,b) result(g)
    integer, intent(in) :: a,b
    integer :: bt, tmp,g
    g=a
    bt=b
    
    do while(bt/=0)
      tmp = bt
      bt = mod(g,bt)
      g = tmp
    end do
  end function 

! A real implementation needs to account for length less than 4, and 
! sequential zeros, but this is omitted for simplicity and being of zero 
! algorithmic interest
 function gcd_array(A) result(g)
   integer, dimension(:), intent(in) :: A
   integer :: g
   type(Divisibility) :: fdiv
   g=0
   do i=1, 4
     g=gcdi(g,A(i)) 
   end do
   ! Shortcut if we have already found a coprime tuple   
   if (g == 1) then
     return
   end if
   
   fdiv = initialise_divisibility(g)

   do i=4,size(A)
     ! If A_i is not divisible by the gcd
     if (.not.fdiv%check(A(i))) then ! Calculate the new gcd
       g = gcdi(A(i),g)
       ! Terminate search if coprime tuple is found
       if (g == 1) then
          exit 
       end if 
       ! Recalculate the divisibility parameters for the new gcd
       fdiv = initialise_divisibility(g)
     end if 
   end do

   
 end function 

end module

program gcdv
  use gcdexample 
  integer, dimension(10) :: v = [6,6,6,6,12,33,39,42,99,102]
  print*,gcd(v)
end program

Q: Is Visual Studio 2022 Consolas font really Consolas? A:

It seems ComboBox with font selection sometimes doesn't update when changing VS theme (VS2022). For me it was displaying invalid font name (Consolas) when Cascadia Mono font was used. For anyone having doubts if ComboBox points to really text editor font I suggest to change ComboBox font to other font and revert to font you want to use, this should reload text editor font. Also keep in mind font selection ComboBox is only for one theme, so when you change theme, or when it automatically changes to other theme (system theme is used) then theme may be changed, but text editor font or ComboBox font may have previous value

Q: systemd apparently not finding .service file A:

Make sure that if you are putting your units in the user folder ~/.config/systemd/user/*.service that you are running the command as

systemctl --user <command>

(note the --user)

Q: Generating image thumbnails in ASP.NET? A:

For intensive server-side code, I suggest you use other techniques than GDI+ that has not been designed to handle images chunk by chunk (in a streaming manner).

You can use Windows Imaging Component or WPF for this task. There is a very good example on how to do this in a fast and - more important - scalable manner here:

The fastest way to resize images from ASP.NET. And it’s (more) supported-ish.
